newsitem.title: USA: Group says safety advocates downplayed airbag risk.
newsitem.headline: Group says safety advocates downplayed airbag risk.

text.p: Consumer advocates urged the government almost four years ago to downplay potential hazards of airbags, including the risk they pose to children and small adults, the Competitive Enterprise Institute said Thursday.

The institute, which opposes the airbag mandate and favors limited government, said consumer and safety groups persuaded the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) to water down an airbag warning in cars.

The safety groups, including Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, urged the NHTSA not to include in its airbag notices a warning about sitting too close to the airbag, according to documents dated February 1993 that the institute released.

The consumer and insurance groups said such a warning might mislead people into believing they should not put their seats in the most forward position even if that positioin suited them best for driving, the documents said.
The institute's general counsel, Sam Kazman, said the safety groups are now reversing themselves and are blaming the auto industry for the watered-down airbag warnings.
"If we're raising doubts about their reliability and credibility, I think those doubts are very much deserved," Kazman told a news conference.
Those consumer advocates testified about airbag safety in a House Appropriations subcommittee Thursday.
Henry Jasny, general counsel for Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety, denied his group had downplayed airbag dangers. He said airbags have saved 1,600 lives.
Although Kazman admitted airbags save lives on balance, he said the government should abandon its airbag requirement.

"No matter how much the technology's improved, the notion that government can get involved here and give us one set of across-the-board requirements for 200 million Americans is in our view crazy," he said.
